title: The Old Tree Behind My Childhood House
script: Narrator: [warmly] Behind my childhood house stood a huge old banyan tree that my grandfather said was already tall before he was even born.
Narrator: [reflective] As kids, my cousins and I climbed its thick branches every afternoon, although our mothers constantly told us to be more careful.
Narrator: [thoughtful] I never really thought about the tree as something fragile, because it had always been there, exactly the same, throughout my whole childhood.
Narrator: [honestly] Last year, a strong storm hit our village, and when I finally visited home again, half the tree had fallen during the heavy wind.
Narrator: [with feeling] I stood there looking at the broken branches for a long time, feeling a sadness I didn't fully expect to feel.
Narrator: [gently] My father noticed me standing there and said, it's just a tree, son, although I could tell even he felt something similar.
Narrator: [reflective] I realized I wasn't only sad about the tree itself, but about how quickly things I assumed were permanent could actually change.
Narrator: [thoughtful] That night, I asked my grandfather if he was sad too, since he had known that tree even longer than my father had.
Narrator: [warmly] He said something I still think about often. He said, nothing in nature is truly permanent, so we should appreciate it while it stands.
Narrator: [softly] The remaining half of the tree is still alive, though smaller now, and new branches have already started growing from where it broke.
Narrator: [hopeful] My father planted a young banyan sapling nearby too, so that eventually, when the old tree finally dies, something will already be growing to replace it.
Narrator: [peacefully] I visited again last month and sat under what remains of that ancient tree, listening to the same birds that used to wake me as a child.
Narrator: [warmly] I think about my grandfather's words whenever I pass any old tree now, because they taught me something simple but important about paying attention while things last.

quiz.question: What kind of tree stood behind the narrator's childhood house?
options: A small palm tree
A huge old banyan tree
A young mango tree
A pine tree
quiz.explanation: A huge old banyan tree stood behind the house, already tall before his grandfather was born.

quiz.question: What happened to the tree during a storm last year?
options: Nothing happened
Half of it fell during heavy wind
It was cut down deliberately
It grew taller
quiz.explanation: A strong storm hit the village, and half the tree had fallen during the heavy wind.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's grandfather say about the tree?
options: Trees should always be cut down eventually
Nothing in nature is truly permanent, so we should appreciate it while it stands
The tree was never important
He never noticed the tree at all
quiz.explanation: His grandfather said nothing in nature is truly permanent, so people should appreciate it while it stands.

quiz.question: What did the narrator's father do after the storm?
options: He removed the remaining tree completely
He planted a young banyan sapling nearby
He built a fence around it
He ignored the damage
quiz.explanation: The father planted a young banyan sapling nearby so something would already be growing when the old tree eventually dies.

quiz.question: What is the narrator's final lesson from this experience?
options: To avoid old trees
To pay attention to things while they last
To never visit his childhood home again
That storms are always destructive with no benefit
quiz.explanation: He concludes his grandfather's words taught him something important about paying attention while things last.
